scope: 21 existing active AQA AS Year 1 Pure Maths school-mock short flashcards: domains, range, inverse exponential/logarithm functions, straight-line gradients, trigonometric exact values and quadrant signs, logarithm laws, increasing derivatives, the integration constant and geometric-series convergence.
eligibility: AQA Year 1 Pure only. Exclude Year 2, Statistics and Mechanics and do not add long worked problems disguised as flashcards.
safeguards: Scope every patch to exact original ID, question, answer, Maths AS, active and mock=true.
Keep existing accepted/rejected examples and all original card properties.
Retain the original 3345 core IDs, saved progress, cloud sync, XP and question banks.
Exercise the production flashcard marker with valid and wrong responses; do not rely on appending strings alone.
limitations: Curated paraphrases are not a proof that every possible student wording is marked correctly.
Does not independently certify that every bullet of the AQA Year 1 Pure mock scope is covered.
More difficult proof, vectors and signed definite-area methods should remain in separate worked exam questions.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What functions are inverses of each other?
accept: The exponential function e^x and natural logarithm ln(x) undo each other on their appropriate domains.
reject: The functions x squared and natural logarithm are mutual inverses over all real x.
The natural logarithm ln(x) is the inverse of y=10^x.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is the domain of a function?
accept: A function's domain is the set of input values it is defined for.
reject: The domain means the set of output values that the function can produce.
Every function must have all real numbers as its domain.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is the range of a function?
accept: The range is the set of outputs the function can actually take.
reject: The range is the set of permitted input values rather than outputs.
The range of every real function must contain all real numbers.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is the domain of f(x) = √x over the real numbers?
accept: For the real-valued square root function f(x)=sqrt(x), x can be zero or positive.
reject: The real domain of sqrt(x) is x strictly greater than zero, excluding zero.
For real sqrt(x), the domain is x less than or equal to zero.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is the domain of f(x) = 1/(x−2)?
accept: Every real input is allowed except x=2, where the denominator vanishes.
reject: The domain is all real numbers including x=2.
All real inputs except x=-2, as the excluded input is negative two.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: How are gradients of perpendicular non-vertical lines related?
accept: For two non-vertical perpendicular straight lines their gradients have product minus one.
reject: The gradients of perpendicular non-vertical lines must multiply to positive one.
Perpendicular non-vertical lines must have equal gradients.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: State the point–gradient form of a straight-line equation.
accept: A line through (x1,y1) of gradient m satisfies y-y1=m(x-x1).
reject: Point gradient form is y+y1=m(x+x1).
Point gradient form is y-y1=(x-x1)/m for every gradient m.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: How are gradients of two nonvertical perpendicular lines related?
accept: The product of the gradients of two perpendicular, non-vertical lines is -1.
reject: The gradients of two perpendicular nonvertical lines always sum to zero.
Two perpendicular nonvertical lines always have the same gradient.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is the gradient between (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂)?
accept: Subtract the y-coordinates and divide by the corresponding change in x: (y2-y1)/(x2-x1).
reject: Gradient equals (x2-x1)/(y2-y1), swapping rise and run.
Gradient equals (y2+y1)/(x2+x1), adding rather than subtracting.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is true of the gradients of two non-vertical parallel lines?
accept: Two straight lines are parallel when they have the same gradient, provided both are non-vertical.
reject: The product of gradients of parallel nonvertical lines is always minus one.
Parallel nonvertical lines always have gradients equal in size but opposite in sign.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is the exact value of sin 45°?
accept: Sine of forty-five degrees equals one over square root of two, or sqrt(2)/2.
reject: sin 45 degrees equals sqrt(3)/2.
sin 45 degrees equals 1/2.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is the exact value of cos 30°?
accept: Cosine of thirty degrees equals sqrt(3) divided by two.
reject: cos 30 degrees equals sqrt(2)/2.
cos 30 degrees equals 1/2.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: In which quadrants is sin θ positive?
accept: Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants.
reject: Sine is positive in quadrants III and IV.
Sine is positive in quadrants I and IV.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is logₐ(xᵏ)?
accept: Move the exponent to the front: log base a of x to power k equals k times log base a of x.
reject: log_a(x^k) equals (log_a x)^k.
log_a(x^k) equals log_a(kx) rather than k log_a x.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is logₐ(xy)?
accept: The logarithm of a product is a sum: log_a(xy)=log_a(x)+log_a(y).
reject: log_a(xy)=log_a(x) times log_a(y).
log_a(x+y)=log_a(x)+log_a(y) for any positive x and y.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is logₐ1?
accept: The logarithm base a of one is zero because a raised to zero equals one.
reject: log base a of one equals one for every permitted base.
log base a of one equals a instead of zero.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is logₐa?
accept: The logarithm of its own valid base equals one because a^1=a.
reject: log base a of a equals zero.
log base a of a equals the value a.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: State the logarithm quotient law for logₐ(x/y).
accept: For positive x and y, logarithm base a of x/y equals log_a x minus log_a y.
reject: log_a(x/y)=log_a(x)+log_a(y).
log_a(x/y)=log_a(x)/log_a(y).

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What does f′(x)>0 mean over an interval?
accept: A positive first derivative throughout an interval means the function increases there.
reject: If f prime is positive throughout an interval the function must decrease.
A strictly positive derivative means the graph is stationary at every point in that interval.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: Why is +C needed in an indefinite integral?
rows.originalBack: Differentiation removes constant terms, so every constant shift is an antiderivative.
accept: An indefinite integral needs an arbitrary integration constant because differentiating any constant gives zero.
reject: The added constant is necessary because differentiation of a constant equals one.
A definite integral always needs plus C appended to its numerical result.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: When does an infinite geometric series have a finite sum?
accept: An infinite geometric series converges to a finite sum when the magnitude of r is less than one.
reject: An infinite geometric series converges whenever r is greater than one.
An infinite geometric series has a finite sum when r=-1 because the terms alternate.
